title: Mode Changes Are Unclear
summary: Mode changes are unclear when an interface fails to update the user's mental model at the moment a system state changes. The failure is distinct from general state invisibility and from accumulated spatial memory burden, although the same interface can exhibit all three problems.
keyFacts: A mode error occurs when a user takes an action that is correct for one system state and incorrect for another, without knowing which state they are in.
A mode error requires both a user mental model of system state and an interface failure to update that mental model when the actual state changes.
Mode-change clarity is narrower than general state visibility because it concerns the moment of transition, not only the resulting state.
Mode-change clarity is distinct from layout instability and spatial memory burden, although mode changes that reorganise the interface can cause those problems.
Common mechanisms include insufficient visual differentiation, no perceptible transition event, and confirmation steps calibrated incorrectly to consequence.
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement treated activation state and readiness state as high-consequence mode states in a powered surgical device interface.
In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons reviewed the legacy interface in structured sessions.

The Raymarine prototype comparison recorded wrong domain activations of six of eight under the contextual model and zero of eight under the fixed model, with a 2.30 second median target-browsing cost.
The maritime VTS prototype comparison recorded replay recognition of five of eight in the legacy condition and eight of eight in the prototype under controlled conditions.
Creative Navy does not claim IEC 62366-1 compliance as a deliverable for the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement; summative validation was the manufacturer's responsibility and was not in scope.

bodySections.heading: What unclear mode changes mean
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A mode-change clarity failure is an interface failure in which the transition between system modes is not communicated in a way the user can reliably perceive under real operating conditions. The user may act confidently because the action is correct for the state they believe the system is in. The error occurs because the user's mental model no longer matches the actual system state.

A mode error is not the same as selecting the wrong visible option or misreading a visible value. A mode error requires two conditions at the same time: the user has a mental model of the system's current state, and the interface fails to update that mental model when the actual state changes.

In low-consequence software, mode errors often produce recoverable mistakes. In clinical and safety-critical contexts, mode errors become use-related risk because the user's next action may depend directly on whether the system is active, inactive, ready, unavailable, queued, or pending.

bodySections.heading: Mode errors are failures of transition visibility
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A mode-change clarity failure concerns the transition between modes, not only the visibility of the final state. A system can display its current mode clearly after a transition and still fail if the user does not perceive that the transition occurred.

This distinction matters because many mode errors do not appear dramatic at the interface surface. The interface may show a new state, a visible object may move, or an action may appear to have been accepted. The failure is the quiet mismatch between what the system has done and what the user believes it has done.

Mode-change clarity must be evaluated under the conditions of use. Brief glances, variable lighting, gloves, sterile positioning, divided attention, interruptions, and operational pressure can all reduce whether a state transition is perceptible in practice.

bodySections.heading: Mode-change clarity is narrower than general state visibility
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Mode-change clarity is a specific instance of state visibility failure. General state visibility concerns whether information about what the system is doing is available at the surface. Mode-change clarity concerns whether the transition into a new state is communicated in a way that reliably updates the user's mental model.

The distinction is structurally important. A system can display the current mode in a visible location and still fail if the transition produces no perceptible signal. A mode change can also fail if the visual difference between the previous and current state is too subtle, or if the interface reorganises in a way that prevents immediate orientation.

Mode-change clarity is also distinct from the cognitive failure in which the interface demands too much memory. Mode changes that reorganise the interface can create layout instability, but the transition-specific failure is the event of failing to communicate the change. The memory burden is the cumulative cost of maintaining spatial maps across inconsistent view states.

bodySections.heading: Insufficient visual differentiation makes mode changes easy to miss
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The simplest mode-change clarity failure occurs when two or more modes are not visually distinct enough to register without close attention. A standby state and an active state that share layout, iconography, and visual weight may differ only by a small label or colour indicator. Under operational pressure, that difference may not be read or noticed.

Single-channel state communication is a common cause. When colour is the primary indicator, the mode distinction degrades when colour perception degrades. Source examples name variable operating theatre illumination, direct sunlight on a display, and spectral shift from night vision equipment as conditions that can reduce the reliability of colour coding.

The design response is redundant communication. Spatial position, icon form, and colour can each communicate the same state independently. If one channel degrades, the other channels can still support recognition of the mode state.

bodySections.heading: Silent transition events leave the user's mental model unchanged
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A system can show the resulting state clearly and still fail to signal that a transition occurred. If the mode change produces only a static state update, and the difference between states is subtle, the change can pass unnoticed during inattention, physical distraction, or divided focus.

This produces the characteristic mode error pattern. The user operates confidently in a mode they believe to be current because their mental model was accurate until the system silently changed. The failure is not confusion. The failure is an interface update that did not register as a transition.

The design response at transition level includes a perceptible change signal at the moment of transition, sufficient visual distinctiveness between states, and confirmation mechanisms for high-consequence state changes where unintended activation must be prevented.

bodySections.heading: Confirmation steps require consequence-based calibration
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Mode-change confirmation is a calibration problem. Interfaces can over-correct by adding confirmation steps that create friction without reducing risk. Interfaces can also under-correct by allowing high-consequence state changes to proceed without confirmation.

A confirmation step is not protective if the user does not recognise what is being confirmed. Ambiguous confirmation adds cognitive load without preventing the mode error it is intended to prevent. Conversely, a high-consequence activation that proceeds without confirmation relies entirely on the user's attention at the moment of activation.

The appropriate design response is not a uniform confirmation policy. Low-consequence mode changes can proceed without confirmation. High-consequence activations need confirmation mechanisms that are simple enough for divided-attention use, distinctive enough not to be bypassed through habit, and located at the decision point where the user's intended mode is clearest.

bodySections.heading: deSoutter Medical / Zethon shows mode-change clarity in a surgical device context
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement provides a medical-device example of mode-change clarity under operating theatre conditions. The device is a powered ultrasonic bone cutter operating at rotational speeds from approximately 200 rpm to approximately 85,000 rpm, used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery.

The interface was a safety-critical embedded GUI used during live procedures. Surgeons interacted with it briefly, with primary attention on the surgical field and the patient, through gloves, and within a sterile field that constrained positioning and access.

The high-consequence mode states were the transition from inactive to active and from active to inactive. A surgeon who assumes the device is inactive when it has transitioned to active state, or who assumes readiness when a readiness sequence is incomplete, is acting within a false mental model in a context where that model affects use-related risk.

The legacy interface followed the internal software architecture and exposed functions in the order they existed in the software. From a clinical perspective, activation states and readiness conditions were difficult to interpret at a glance, parameters relevant during cutting were visible but not visually prioritised, and warnings were presented as text rather than instantly recognisable patterns.

Eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons familiar with ultrasonic and powered tools reviewed the legacy interface in structured sessions. The failure patterns were consistent across the participant group. Under IEC 62366-1 framing, this interaction profile constituted use-related risk because readiness verification had to happen during brief glances in a live operating theatre.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats mode-change clarity as an operating-conditions problem
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses unclear mode changes by defining the operating conditions under which each transition must be perceived, then translating those requirements into structural interface standards.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For mode-change clarity, domain learning establishes when transitions occur in real operation, what the user is doing at those moments, which senses and actions are constrained, and what consequence follows if the transition is missed. In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, the requirement became specific: activation state had to be recognisable without reading during brief glances, under variable theatre lighting, with gloved hands, divided attention, and sterile field constraints.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, Creative Navy reviewed 12 human factors studies and ergonomics papers covering touch performance with gloved hands, visual search under time pressure, and attention switching in dual-task conditions. Thirteen structured sessions with the same eight surgeons combined interviews with procedural walkthroughs.

The resulting operational model specified which transitions had to be perceptible in a brief glance, under variable lighting, at relevant viewing angles, and under divided attention. The design standard required every critical mode state to be distinguishable through recognition without reading, using independent redundant cues.

Spatial stability gave critical indicators fixed positions across screens and mode states. Icon form provided distinct shapes that did not depend on colour. Reserved colour, applied consistently to each state and not used for other purposes, provided a third cue. No single channel failure was allowed to make a critical mode state ambiguous.

Intermediate confirmation steps were also calibrated against the operational model. Steps that added cognitive burden without contributing to safety were removed. Steps retained for protective function were redesigned for completion under divided-attention clinical use.

Eight surgeons in structured review sessions reported two changes compared with the legacy interface: device state could be verified during brief glances without reading, and speed and parameter adjustments no longer interrupted surgical workflow. These are surgeon-reported outcomes from participants in the design engagement, not post-deployment operational measurements.

The engagement produced a documented usability engineering trail structured to support IEC 62366-1 verification and validation activities. Summative validation was the manufacturer's responsibility and was not in scope for this engagement. Creative Navy does not claim IEC 62366-1 compliance as a deliverable for the engagement.

bodySections.heading: Additional engagement evidence shows different forms of mode-change failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Raymarine provides a prototype comparison where a control changed functional domain without a sufficiently clear mode boundary. In the Ray53, Ray63 and Ray73 line context, a promising AIS concept used the lower encoder to move between vessel targets, while the same encoder had already been assigned as the primary channel selector in the radio view and would have had a third role in settings. When an alert interrupted an interaction, it became unclear whether the next rotation would select a vessel, change the tuned channel, or navigate a message.

Creative Navy designed the Raymarine test protocols, moderated all twenty-four sessions, and analysed the results. Raymarine supplied the physical bench mockup. The comparison was paired and counterbalanced within participants, with task wording, target data, and starting states held constant. Wrong domain activations were six of eight under the contextual model and zero of eight under the fixed model on the retune task, and again on the recovery task. The fixed-role control model carried a cost of 2.30 seconds of median target browsing. These findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture, not radio performance, real-world calling accuracy, or outcomes at sea.

Schone Airspace Group provides an example where requested mode and reported mode had to remain distinct. In Mission Control, a command branch with a healthy link sent a request, received an acknowledgement three seconds later while the aircraft was still reporting its previous flight mode, and received fresh telemetry reporting the requested mode three seconds after that. The interface rule was that the shown mode was the mode the aircraft reported, never the mode the operator requested. The product was built and is in test, not deployed or in operational use.

Streetec GmbH and kntrl 2 provide an example of deliberately separating two change models in one interface. Manual adjustments execute immediately. Preset edits require explicit saving. Switching modes while the vehicle is moving requires confirmation. The distinction prevents users from treating a saved-change context and an immediate-change context as the same mode of operation.

AIT, a European manufacturer of residential and commercial heat pumps, provides a designed status model for queued modes. Heating, cooling, domestic hot water, pool, photovoltaics, and ventilation were operating modes, with ventilation not yet supported at the time. Only one heat-generating mode runs at a time, while photovoltaics and ventilation can run alongside one. A requested heat-generating mode may therefore be queued behind another. The designed widget status indicators distinguished in focus, mode active, and mode queued.

A European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells provides an audit example. Each cell element could be set automatic or manual independently, determining whether the system assigned it work. An operator leaving a shift had to set modes correctly for unattended running. Creative Navy's review found that a storage tile combined a green transporting header band with a solid red selected icon, while the only other selection cue was a near-imperceptible border change. Four states were encoded by header colour alone at approximately 10px with no legend. The product is in development.

A European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them provides a safety-engineering example where requested state must not visually replace confirmed state before the vehicle reports the result. Armament state was specified as five explicit values: safe, armed, change pending, unavailable, and unknown. Armament state was its own axis and not a mode. The handheld interface was built; nothing was measured.

A European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators provides an example where a mode was visible and still missed. In the replay condition, the historical indicator sat inside the time controls and lost salience as the operator inspected detail. The selected prototype model marked the entire relevant workspace as historical, showed recording time, coverage, and gaps, made linked inspectors inherit the same time context, and made Return to Live a deliberate action. In Creative Navy-measured controlled prototype testing with eight participants using sanitised training scenarios, correct initial replay recognition was five of eight in the legacy condition and eight of eight in the prototype. Six of the eight participants had earlier programme exposure, and the result has no significance test or confidence interval.

bodySections.heading: Mode-change clarity has specific boundaries
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Mode-change clarity does not mean every mode change needs a confirmation step. Confirmation is appropriate when the consequence profile justifies it. Confirmation is harmful when it adds cognitive load without protecting against the mode error likely in the operating scenario.

Mode-change clarity does not mean colour cannot be used. The failure occurs when colour is the primary or only state channel for a critical mode distinction. Colour can be one redundant cue when spatial position and icon form also communicate the state independently.

Mode-change clarity does not replace general state visibility. A system still needs current state to be available at the surface. This page covers the narrower event-level failure: the transition itself is not perceptible enough to update the user's mental model.

The engagement evidence has different strengths and must not be blended. The deSoutter Medical / Zethon outcomes are surgeon-reported from structured review sessions and not post-deployment operational measurement. Raymarine and maritime VTS figures are controlled prototype findings, not field outcomes. AIT decisions describe what was designed, not measured results. The industrial example is an audit finding for a product in development. The handheld C2 work was specified and built, with no measured result stated.
